intro: Every group of people in the world has special days. They light lamps, dance in parades, cook favorite foods and remember loved ones. They also play games, sing songs and tell stories. These things make up a big part of a people's culture, or way of life.

In this unit you will visit Carnival in Brazil, Lunar New Year in China and Korea, Diwali in India and Día de los Muertos in Mexico. You will hear mariachi and flamenco, play chess and soccer, and meet Anansi and the Monkey King. You will also see festivals right here in Chicago.

By the end, you will be able to explain why people celebrate. You will compare two traditions from different places. You will also trace how music, games and stories travel and blend into something new.
bigQuestion: What can the ways people celebrate, play and tell stories teach us about what they care about?

title: Festivals, Arts and Everyday Life

chapters.title: Festivals and Celebrations
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people all over the world stop their busy lives to celebrate together?

story.title: The Sugar Skull
story.kicker: Lucía thinks a skull will be scary. Her grandmother shows her it is full of love.
paragraphs: It is the end of October in Pilsen, a Mexican American neighborhood in Chicago. Lucía sits at her grandmother's kitchen table. In front of her is a small white skull. It is made of sugar. Lucía frowns. Why would anyone want a skull?

Her grandmother, Abuela Rosa, smiles. She hands Lucía a tube of pink icing. "We decorate it," she says. "Flowers for the eyes. A big smile. Then we write a name on the forehead." Lucía asks whose name. "Your grandfather's," Abuela says softly.

Lucía draws blue petals around the eyes. She adds yellow dots and a curly smile. Abuela writes "Tomás" across the top. The skull no longer looks scary. It looks cheerful, like Grandpa Tomás did when he laughed.

In the living room, Abuela has built a table with photos, candles and orange marigolds. She sets the skull next to Grandpa's picture. She adds a cup of his favorite hot chocolate. "This is our ofrenda," she says. "On Día de los Muertos, we remember the people we love."

Lucía looks at the photo and the bright skull. She feels a little sad. She also feels close to her grandfather. Abuela squeezes her hand. "Remembering is a way of loving," she says. Lucía nods. Next year, she wants to make one herself.
story.think: How did the sugar skull change for Lucía from the start of the story to the end?

lessons.title: Carnival in Brazil
lessons.mainIdea: Carnival in Brazil is a huge festival of music, dancing and costumes held just before Lent.
reading: Picture a street in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Drums pound. Thousands of dancers wear feathers and sequins. Giant floats roll by. People on the sidewalks sing and dance too. This is *Carnival*, one of the biggest parties on Earth.

Carnival comes just before Lent. Lent is a season of about forty days in the Christian calendar. Many Christians give something up during Lent. So people celebrate with joy before it starts. Carnival lasts several days in February or March.

In Rio, groups called *samba schools* practice all year. They build floats and sew costumes. Then they parade and dance to samba music. Samba grew from the music of Afro-Brazilian communities. Judges pick a winning school. Other Brazilian cities have their own Carnival styles.

words.d: a festival of parades, music and costumes held just before Lent
groups in Brazil that practice all year to parade and dance at Carnival
a special time when a community celebrates together

look.title: The Samba School Workshop
look.text: It is August in Rio. Carnival is months away. In a big warehouse, people glue feathers onto a costume. Others paint a float shaped like a giant bird. A drummer practices the same beat again and again. Nobody is paid to do all of it. They come because they love their neighborhood's school.
look.prompt: Why do you think people work for a whole year on a parade that lasts one night?

check.q: When does Carnival happen?
choices: In the middle of summer vacation in July
check.why: The reading says Carnival comes just before Lent, the Christian season of about forty days.

check.q: What is a samba school in Brazil?
choices: A school where children learn math
A group that practices all year to parade at Carnival
check.why: Samba schools are groups that build floats, sew costumes and dance in the Carnival parade.

check.q: Samba music grew from the music of which communities?
check.why: The reading says samba grew from the music of Afro-Brazilian communities.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year in China
lessons.mainIdea: In China, the Spring Festival welcomes the new year of the moon calendar with family, food and the color red.
reading: Mei's family cleans every corner of their home in Beijing. They hang red paper on the doors. Red stands for good luck. Tomorrow is the *Spring Festival*. It is China's biggest holiday. Many people call it Lunar New Year.

The date comes from a *lunar calendar*. A lunar calendar follows the moon. So the holiday moves each year. It falls in January or February. Each year is also named for one of twelve animals, like the dragon or the rabbit.

Families travel far to be together. On New Year's Eve they share a big dinner. In the north, many families fold dumplings. Children get red envelopes with money inside. Lion dances and fireworks fill the streets. The festival ends about fifteen days later with the Lantern Festival.

words.d: the Chinese name for Lunar New Year, China's biggest holiday
a calendar that counts months by the moon

look.title: The Red Envelope
look.text: Grandma hands Mei a small red envelope with gold letters. Mei says a New Year wish for her grandmother's good health. Inside is some money. Mei knows the red color is a wish for good luck. She thanks her grandmother with both hands.
look.prompt: What does the red envelope tell you about what families hope for at New Year?

check.q: Why does the date of Lunar New Year change each year?
choices: The government picks a new day
It follows a lunar calendar based on the moon
It is always on the first snow
check.why: Lunar New Year follows a lunar calendar, which counts months by the moon, so the date moves.

check.q: What does the color red stand for at the Spring Festival?
check.why: The reading says red stands for good luck, so families hang red paper and give red envelopes.

check.q: What festival ends the New Year season in China?
check.why: The Spring Festival season ends about fifteen days later with the Lantern Festival.

lessons.title: Seollal in Korea
lessons.mainIdea: Korea celebrates Lunar New Year as Seollal, with bows of respect to elders and a bowl of rice cake soup.
reading: Ji-woo puts on a bright *hanbok*. A hanbok is traditional Korean clothing. Today is *Seollal*, the Korean Lunar New Year. Ji-woo and her brother kneel before their grandparents. They bow all the way to the floor.

This deep bow is called sebae. It shows respect for elders. After the bow, the grandparents give good wishes for the year. They often give the children a little money too. Many families also honor their ancestors on this day.

Then everyone eats tteokguk. It is a soup with thin slices of rice cake. Many Koreans say eating it makes you one year older. China and Korea usually share the same holiday date. Yet each country celebrates in its own way.

words.d: the Korean name for Lunar New Year
traditional Korean clothing, often worn on holidays
older people in a family or community

look.title: Two New Years, Side by Side
look.text: In Beijing, a family eats dumplings and watches fireworks. In Seoul, a family bows to the grandparents and eats rice cake soup. Both families are celebrating the same new moon. Both are wishing for a good year.
look.prompt: Name one thing that is the same and one thing that is different about the two families.

check.q: What is sebae?
choices: A deep bow to elders at Seollal
check.why: Sebae is the deep New Year bow that shows respect for elders.

check.q: What food do many Korean families eat at Seollal?
check.why: The reading says families eat tteokguk, a soup with thin slices of rice cake.

check.q: How are Seollal and the Chinese Spring Festival alike?
choices: Both follow the lunar calendar and usually fall on the same date
Both are harvest festivals in fall
check.why: China and Korea usually share the same Lunar New Year date, but each celebrates in its own way.

lessons.title: Diwali, the Festival of Lights
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali is a festival of lights celebrated in India and around the world by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains.
reading: At dusk in Jaipur, India, Priya sets small clay lamps along the steps of her home. Each lamp is called a *diya*. Soon hundreds of little flames glow down the street. It is *Diwali*, the festival of lights.

Diwali comes in October or November. It lasts about five days. Hindus, Sikhs and Jains all celebrate it, each with their own stories. Many Hindus remember the god Rama returning home. People lit lamps to welcome him. The lights stand for good winning over evil.

Families clean their homes and wear new clothes. They share sweets with neighbors. Many make *rangoli* at the doorway. Rangoli are bright patterns made from colored powder, rice or flowers. Many families also pray for a good year ahead.

words.d: a festival of lights celebrated in the fall by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains
a small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali
colorful patterns made on the floor from powder, rice or flowers

look.title: A Rangoli at the Door
look.text: On the floor by the front door is a circle of color. Pink, orange and green powder form a flower with eight petals. A diya burns in the center. Priya's mother drew it this morning. Guests step around it carefully as they arrive.
look.prompt: Why might a family put something beautiful right at the front door?

check.q: What do the lights of Diwali stand for?
check.why: The reading says the lights stand for good winning over evil.

check.q: Which groups celebrate Diwali?
check.why: Hindus, Sikhs and Jains all celebrate Diwali, each with their own stories.

check.q: What is a diya?
check.why: A diya is a small clay oil lamp lit at Diwali.

lessons.title: Día de los Muertos in Mexico
lessons.mainIdea: On Día de los Muertos, families in Mexico remember loved ones who have died, with altars, flowers and food.
reading: Remember Lucía's sugar skull? She was getting ready for *Día de los Muertos*. The name means Day of the Dead. It is celebrated on November 1 and 2. It began in Mexico and blends Indigenous and Catholic traditions.

Families build an *ofrenda*. An ofrenda is an altar with photos of loved ones who have died. They add candles, the person's favorite foods and sweet bread called pan de muerto. Orange marigolds light the way with their color and smell.

Many families visit the cemetery. They clean the graves and decorate them with flowers. Some stay late, sharing food and stories. The day is not meant to be scary. It is a way to say that the people we love are still remembered.

words.d: the Day of the Dead, a Mexican holiday on November 1 and 2 for remembering loved ones
a home altar with photos, candles, flowers and food for loved ones who have died
a way of doing things that is passed down from older people to younger people

look.title: A Poet Looks at Death and Fiesta
look.text: The Mexican poet Octavio Paz wrote that many Mexicans do not hide from death. They talk about it, joke about it, and even celebrate it. He saw this as a close, honest relationship with the end of life.
look.cite: Octavio Paz, The Labyrinth of Solitude, 1950
look.prompt: How does Paz's idea help explain why sugar skulls have happy smiles?

check.q: When is Día de los Muertos celebrated?
check.why: The reading says Día de los Muertos is on November 1 and 2.

check.q: What is an ofrenda?
choices: A home altar with photos, candles and food
check.why: An ofrenda is an altar that holds photos of loved ones, candles, flowers and food.

check.q: What is the main purpose of Día de los Muertos?
choices: To celebrate the harvest of corn
To remember loved ones who have died
check.why: The day is a way to remember and honor loved ones, not to frighten anyone.

lessons.title: Oktoberfest in Germany
lessons.mainIdea: Oktoberfest in Munich began with a royal wedding in 1810 and grew into a giant fair of food, music and rides.
reading: In 1810, Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria married Princess Therese. The city of Munich threw a party in a big field. There was a horse race. Everyone was invited. People liked it so much that they did it again the next year.

That party became *Oktoberfest*. Today it starts in late September and ends in early October. Millions of visitors come. They ride a Ferris wheel and roller coasters. They eat big soft pretzels and roast chicken. Brass bands play in huge tents.

Many people wear *traditional dress* from Bavaria. Men may wear leather shorts called lederhosen. Women may wear a dress and apron called a dirndl. Other cities, including some in the United States, now hold their own Oktoberfests.

words.d: a yearly fair in Munich, Germany, that began with a royal wedding in 1810
clothing worn in a place for a long time, often on special days

look.title: How Long Do Festivals Last?
rows: Lunar New Year season in China
look.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles on each festival; Oktoberfest length varies from 16 to 18 days
look.prompt: Which festival lasts the longest? Which is the shortest?

check.why: Oktoberfest began as a party for the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese.

check.q: In which city is the famous Oktoberfest held?
check.why: The reading says Oktoberfest takes place in Munich, in the German region of Bavaria.

check.q: Look at the chart. Which lasts about 5 days?

lessons.title: Cherry Blossom Season in Japan
lessons.mainIdea: In spring, people in Japan gather under blooming cherry trees for hanami, a custom of enjoying the flowers.
reading: In early spring, the cherry trees in a Tokyo park burst into pale pink. Families spread blue mats on the grass. Friends share rice balls and tea. Petals drift down like snow. This custom is called *hanami*, which means flower viewing.
Cherry blossoms are called *sakura*. They bloom for only a week or two. Then the petals fall. Many people in Japan see this as a reminder. Beautiful things do not last forever, so enjoy them now.

The flowers open first in the warm south and later in the cool north. TV news shows maps of where the trees are blooming. People have enjoyed hanami for more than a thousand years. In 1912, Tokyo gave cherry trees to Washington, D.C., as a gift of friendship.

words.d: the Japanese custom of gathering to enjoy blooming flowers, especially cherry blossoms
the Japanese word for cherry blossoms
something a group of people usually does, often for a long time

look.title: The Blossom Front
look.text: Picture a map of Japan. In late March, the pink dots appear in the south. A week later, they move up to Tokyo. By early May, they reach the far north. People watch the pink line move up the map like a slow wave.
look.prompt: Why do the cherry trees bloom later in the north of Japan?

check.q: What does hanami mean?
check.why: Hanami means flower viewing, the custom of enjoying cherry blossoms.

check.q: Why do many people in Japan see cherry blossoms as a reminder?
choices: They last only a short time, so enjoy beauty now
check.why: Sakura bloom for only a week or two, reminding people that beautiful things do not last.

check.q: What did Tokyo give Washington, D.C., in 1912?
check.why: In 1912 Tokyo gave cherry trees to Washington, D.C., as a gift of friendship.

lessons.title: Independence Days
lessons.mainIdea: Many countries celebrate the day they became free to govern themselves.
reading: On July 4, fireworks burst over towns across the United States. The day marks 1776. That year, leaders approved the Declaration of Independence. It said the colonies were free from Britain. A day like this is called an *Independence Day*.

Other nations have their own. Mexico celebrates on September 16. In 1810, a priest named Miguel Hidalgo rang a church bell and called for freedom. Brazil celebrates on September 7, from 1822. India celebrates on August 15, from 1947.

These days share some things. There are flags, parades and speeches. Families picnic and watch fireworks. Each one helps a country remember its *history*. It also tells people they belong to one nation.

words.d: a holiday that marks the day a country became free to govern itself
the true story of what happened in the past

look.title: John Adams Imagines the Fourth of July
look.text: John Adams wrote to his wife Abigail that this day should be celebrated forever. He hoped for parades, games, sports, bells, bonfires and lights, from one end of the country to the other.
look.cite: John Adams, letter to Abigail Adams, July 3, 1776
look.prompt: Which of the things Adams hoped for do people still do on the Fourth of July?

check.q: What happened in 1776 that Americans remember on July 4?
choices: The Declaration of Independence was approved
check.why: July 4 marks 1776, when leaders approved the Declaration of Independence.

check.q: Who rang a church bell in 1810 to call for Mexico's freedom?
check.why: Miguel Hidalgo, a priest, rang a church bell in 1810 and called for freedom.

check.q: Which country celebrates Independence Day on August 15?
check.why: India celebrates on August 15, the day it became independent in 1947.

lessons.title: Four Reasons to Celebrate
lessons.mainIdea: Most festivals celebrate the harvest, history, family or faith, and many celebrate more than one.
reading: Look back at the festivals in this chapter. Why do people hold them? Most have one of four reasons. The first is the *harvest*. The harvest is when crops are gathered. In Korea, the fall holiday Chuseok gives thanks for the harvest.
The second reason is history. Independence Days remember big events in a nation's past. The third reason is family. Lunar New Year brings families home. Día de los Muertos keeps loved ones in memory.

The fourth reason is *faith*. Faith means religious belief. Diwali and the season before Lent come from religious calendars. Many festivals mix reasons. Diwali is about faith, family and a fresh start. Knowing the reasons helps you understand a festival from the inside.

words.d: the time when crops are gathered from the fields
religious belief and the practices that go with it

look.title: Sort the Festivals
look.text: Here are four festivals: Chuseok in Korea, the Fourth of July, Lunar New Year, and Diwali. Here are four reasons: harvest, history, family, faith. Some festivals fit more than one reason.
look.prompt: Match each festival to the reason that fits it best. Which one fits more than one reason?

check.why: The reading names Chuseok as Korea's fall harvest holiday.

check.q: Which is the best example of a festival about history?
check.why: Independence Days remember big events in a nation's past, so they are about history.

check.q: What does the reading say about many festivals?
choices: They mix more than one reason
check.why: The reading says many festivals mix reasons, like Diwali mixing faith, family and a fresh start.

lessons.title: Chicago's Parades and Festivals
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's neighborhoods hold parades and festivals that share the cultures of the people who live there.
reading: Every March, Chicago dyes its river bright green for St. Patrick's Day. The city has done this since 1962. Crowds wear green and watch a parade downtown. The holiday honors Irish heritage. Chicago has a large Irish American community.

Every August, the Bud Billiken Parade marches through Bronzeville on the South Side. It began in 1929. It celebrates Black children and the start of the school year. Bands, drill teams and dancers fill the street.

Many other *neighborhood* festivals happen too. Chinatown holds a Lunar New Year parade with lion dances. Pilsen and Little Village celebrate Mexican Independence. Humboldt Park hosts the Puerto Rican festival each June. Each one shares a *heritage* with the whole city.

words.d: a part of a city where people live near one another
the traditions, language and history that a group passes down
a line of people, bands and floats that moves through the street to celebrate

look.title: A Year of Chicago Festivals
look.text: Winter: a lion dances down the street in Chinatown. March: the river turns green. June: Puerto Rican flags wave in Humboldt Park. August: marching bands step through Bronzeville. September: Mexican flags fill 26th Street in Little Village.
look.prompt: Which of these festivals would you like to visit, and what would you want to learn there?

chapters.title: Music, Games and Stories
chapters.bigQuestion: How do music, games and stories travel around the world and become part of new places?

story.title: One Ball, Five Countries
story.kicker: A single soccer ball travels the world and joins five different games.
paragraphs: The ball starts in a small factory in Sialkot, Pakistan. Many of the world's hand-stitched soccer balls have been made in this city. A worker pulls the last stitch tight. The ball is round and white with black patches. It goes into a box and onto a ship.

In Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, a boy named Davi gets the ball for his birthday. He plays barefoot on the beach with his cousins. They juggle it with their knees and heads. When Davi's family moves away, he gives the ball to his best friend's older brother.

The brother takes it to Lagos, Nigeria, where he goes to college. Kids on a dusty lot use two sandals for a goal. They shout in Yoruba and English. The ball gets scuffed and gray. A visiting teacher from England admires their skill. She is given the ball as a thank-you gift.

In a park in London, her nephew kicks it with friends after school. Later, he moves with his family to Seoul, South Korea. There the ball rolls across a school field. Children cheer in Korean. Last of all, it flies to Chicago, where a girl named Amara plays in Humboldt Park.

The ball is worn out now. Its seams are loose. But it has heard many languages. Every child who kicked it knew the same rules. Nobody needed a translator to play. Amara holds the old ball and wonders where it will go next.
story.think: Why could children in five countries play with the same ball without speaking the same language?

lessons.title: Mariachi from Mexico
lessons.mainIdea: Mariachi is a kind of Mexican music played by a group with violins, trumpets and guitars.
reading: A wedding party dances in Guadalajara, Mexico. Suddenly, a group of musicians walks in. They wear matching suits with silver buttons and wide hats. Trumpets ring out. Violins sing. This is a *mariachi* band.

Mariachi music comes from western Mexico, especially the state of Jalisco. A band often has violins, trumpets and several kinds of guitar. One is the guitarrón, a very large guitar that plays the low notes. The musicians sing too.

Mariachi bands play at birthdays, weddings and holidays. In 2011, UNESCO added mariachi to its list of important living traditions. UNESCO is part of the United Nations. Today mariachi bands play all over the world, including in Chicago.

words.d: a Mexican music group with violins, trumpets and guitars, or the music it plays
a tool for making music, such as a violin, drum or guitar

look.title: Who Plays What?
look.text: In a mariachi band, the violins play the sweet melody. The trumpets play loud, bright parts. The guitars keep the rhythm steady. The guitarrón plays the deep, low notes that you feel in your chest.
look.prompt: If you joined a mariachi band, which instrument would you pick, and why?

check.q: Which Mexican state is most tied to mariachi music?
check.why: The reading says mariachi comes from western Mexico, especially the state of Jalisco.

check.q: What is the guitarrón?
choices: A very large guitar that plays low notes
check.why: The guitarrón is a very large guitar that plays the low notes in a mariachi band.

check.q: Where do mariachi bands often play?
check.why: The reading says mariachi bands play at birthdays, weddings and holidays.

lessons.title: Flamenco from Spain
lessons.mainIdea: Flamenco is a music and dance from southern Spain, shaped strongly by the Roma people of Andalusia.
reading: In Seville, Spain, a dancer stands very still. A guitarist begins to play. A singer lets out a long, deep cry. Then the dancer's heels strike the floor, fast as rain. People around her clap in sharp rhythms. This is *flamenco*.

Flamenco comes from Andalusia, in southern Spain. The Roma people, called Gitanos in Spain, did much to create it. Their music mixed with other traditions of the region. Flamenco has three main parts: singing, guitar and dance.

Flamenco songs can be joyful or full of sorrow. Hand clapping, called palmas, keeps the *rhythm*. Dancers stamp their feet to add sound. In 2010, UNESCO named flamenco an important living tradition too.

words.d: a music and dance from southern Spain with singing, guitar, clapping and stamping
the pattern of strong and soft beats in music
a people with roots in India who have lived across Europe for centuries

look.title: Clap the Pattern
look.text: Try this: count to twelve, over and over. Clap loud on 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Clap soft on the other numbers. Many flamenco songs use a twelve-beat pattern with strong beats in places like these.
look.prompt: Try the clapping pattern. How is it different from clapping a steady one-two-one-two?

check.q: What are the three main parts of flamenco?
check.why: The reading says flamenco has three main parts: singing, guitar and dance.

check.q: Which people did much to create flamenco?
check.why: The Roma people of Andalusia, called Gitanos in Spain, did much to create flamenco.

check.q: What is palmas in flamenco?
choices: Hand clapping that keeps the rhythm
check.why: Palmas is the hand clapping that keeps the rhythm in flamenco.

lessons.title: K-pop from South Korea
lessons.mainIdea: K-pop is popular music from South Korea that mixes many styles and is now loved around the world.
reading: In a stadium in Los Angeles, fans wave glowing sticks. They sing along in Korean, even if they do not speak it. On stage, seven singers dance in perfect step. They are BTS, a *K-pop* group from South Korea.

K-pop means Korean popular music. It took off in the 1990s. It blends pop, hip-hop, rock and dance music. Groups train for years in singing and dancing. Their music videos are bright and carefully planned.

The internet helped K-pop spread. Fans in Brazil, India and Chicago can watch a new video the day it comes out. K-pop borrowed from American music. Now American artists borrow from K-pop. Music can travel both ways.

words.d: popular music from South Korea that mixes pop, hip-hop, rock and dance
music that many people enjoy and buy or stream, like pop songs

look.title: A Two-Way Street
look.text: Hip-hop began in New York City in the 1970s. Years later, Korean songwriters added hip-hop beats to K-pop songs. Then K-pop groups toured the United States. American fans began learning Korean words from the songs.
look.prompt: Explain how music traveled in both directions in this example.

check.q: What does K-pop stand for?
check.why: K-pop means Korean popular music.

check.q: What helped K-pop spread around the world?
check.why: The reading says the internet helped K-pop spread, since fans anywhere can watch new videos.

check.q: Which idea does the K-pop lesson show?
choices: Music can travel in both directions
check.why: K-pop borrowed from American music, and now American artists borrow from K-pop.

lessons.title: The Sitar and the Talking Drum
lessons.mainIdea: The Indian sitar and the West African talking drum are instruments with special sounds and long histories.
reading: The *sitar* is a stringed instrument from India. It has a long wooden neck and a round body, often made from a gourd. Some strings are plucked. Others ring on their own, making a shimmering sound. Ravi Shankar made the sitar famous around the world in the 1960s.

The *talking drum* comes from West Africa. It is shaped like an hourglass. Cords run from one drumhead to the other. A drummer holds it under one arm. Squeezing the cords makes the sound go higher. Letting go makes it lower.

Many West African languages, like Yoruba, are tonal. That means a word's meaning changes with high or low sound. A skilled drummer can copy those sounds. Listeners can recognize names and messages. The drum can almost talk.

words.d: a long-necked stringed instrument from India
an hourglass-shaped drum from West Africa that can copy the rise and fall of speech
describes a language where high or low sound changes a word's meaning

look.title: Squeeze and Listen
look.text: A drummer in Nigeria taps the talking drum. At first the tone is low. He squeezes the cords under his arm. The next taps rise higher. He lets go and they fall. High, low, high, high, low. The pattern matches the tones of someone's name.
look.prompt: How does squeezing the cords help the drum sound like a voice?

check.q: How does a drummer make the talking drum sound higher?
choices: By hitting it with a guitar
check.why: Squeezing the cords tightens the drumheads, so the sound goes higher.

check.q: Who made the sitar famous around the world in the 1960s?
check.why: The reading says Ravi Shankar made the sitar famous around the world in the 1960s.

check.q: What is a tonal language?
choices: A language where high or low sound changes a word's meaning
A language spoken only by drummers
check.why: In a tonal language like Yoruba, the rise and fall of sound changes meaning, which the drum can copy.

lessons.title: Soccer Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: Soccer, called football in most countries, is the world's most popular sport and is easy to play almost anywhere.
reading: Most of the world calls it football. In the United States it is called *soccer*. Kicking-ball games are very old in many lands. The modern rules were written in England in 1863. A group called the Football Association wrote them.

Soccer is simple to start. You need a ball and something for goals. Two sandals or two rocks will do. That is one reason it spread so fast. Sailors, workers and students carried it to South America, Africa and Asia.

Every four years, national teams play in the men's *World Cup*. A women's World Cup is held too. Brazil has won the men's cup more than any other country. Stars like Pelé of Brazil made fans on every continent.

words.d: a game where two teams kick a ball to score in a goal; called football in most countries
a soccer tournament held every four years between national teams

look.title: Men's World Cup Titles
look.cite: FIFA, list of FIFA World Cup winners, 2022
look.prompt: Which country has won the most men's World Cups? How many more than Argentina?

check.q: Where were the modern rules of soccer written in 1863?
check.why: The Football Association in England wrote the modern rules in 1863.

check.q: Why did soccer spread so fast?
choices: It needs only a ball and something for goals
It needs a large ice rink
check.why: Soccer is simple to start; two sandals or rocks can be the goals.

check.q: Look at the chart. Which country has won the most men's World Cups?
check.why: The chart shows Brazil with 5 titles, more than any other country.

lessons.title: Cricket and Baseball
lessons.mainIdea: Cricket is a giant sport in India, and baseball is loved in Japan and the Dominican Republic.
reading: In a Mumbai street, kids use a crate for a wicket. A boy runs up and bowls the ball. The batter swings a flat bat. This is *cricket*. It came to India from Britain. Today India has more cricket fans than any other country.
Cricket and *baseball* are cousins. In both, one player throws, one bats and the batter's team scores runs. India won cricket's World Cup in 1983 and 2011. Huge crowds pack the stadiums.

Baseball began in the United States. An American teacher, Horace Wilson, taught it in Japan in the 1870s. Japan now has a top professional league. The Dominican Republic loves baseball too. Many Major League players were born there. Some stars come from Japan, like Shohei Ohtani.

words.d: a bat-and-ball game from England, very popular in India, Pakistan, Australia and England
a bat-and-ball game from the United States, also loved in Japan and the Dominican Republic
paid to do something as a job, like a professional player

look.title: Cousins on the Field
look.text: Cricket: the bowler throws with a straight arm, and the ball usually bounces first. The bat is flat. Batters run between two wickets. Baseball: the pitcher throws without a bounce. The bat is round. Batters run around four bases.
look.prompt: List two ways cricket and baseball are alike and two ways they are different.

check.q: How did cricket come to India?
check.why: The reading says cricket came to India from Britain.

check.q: Who taught baseball in Japan in the 1870s?
check.why: Horace Wilson, an American teacher, taught baseball in Japan in the 1870s.

check.q: How are cricket and baseball alike?
choices: Both use a round ball kicked with the feet
Both use a net in the middle
One player throws, one bats and the batter's team scores runs
check.why: In both games one player throws, one bats and the batting team scores runs.

lessons.title: Chess from India and Persia
lessons.mainIdea: Chess began in India as chaturanga, grew in Persia, and spread around the world.
reading: Two players sit over a board of 64 squares. They move kings, queens, knights and pawns. This game is *chess*. It is played in parks, schools and online in nearly every country. But where did it start?

Most historians trace chess to India about 1,400 years ago. There it was called *chaturanga*. The pieces stood for parts of an army: foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots. Chaturanga then traveled to Persia, today's Iran. There it was called shatranj.

From Persia, the game spread to Arab lands and then to Europe. Along the way, pieces changed. The Persian adviser piece became the queen. Our word checkmate comes from the Persian shah mat. It means the king is helpless.

words.d: a board game for two where each player tries to trap the other's king
an early form of chess from India, with pieces like an army

look.title: Counting the Chessboard
look.cite: FIDE (International Chess Federation), Laws of Chess, 2023
look.prompt: If each player has 16 pieces and 8 are pawns, how many pieces are not pawns?

check.q: Where do most historians say chess began?
check.why: Most historians trace chess to chaturanga in India about 1,400 years ago.

check.q: What does checkmate come from?
choices: The Persian words shah mat, meaning the king is helpless
check.why: Checkmate comes from the Persian shah mat, which means the king is helpless.

check.q: What did the pieces of chaturanga stand for?
check.why: Chaturanga's pieces stood for parts of an army: foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots.

lessons.title: Anansi the Spider
lessons.mainIdea: Anansi is a clever spider from the folktales of the Akan people of Ghana, and his stories traveled to the Americas.
reading: A grandfather in Ghana sits under a tree. Children crowd around. "This is an Anansi story," he says. They lean in. Anansi is a small spider. He is not strong, but he is very clever. He uses tricks to beat bigger animals.

Anansi stories come from the Akan people of Ghana. They are *folktales*. A folktale is a story told out loud and passed down for many years. In one famous tale, Anansi wins all the world's stories from the Sky God, Nyame.

Enslaved Africans carried Anansi stories across the ocean. The tales lived on in Jamaica and other parts of the Caribbean and the Americas. Anansi is a *trickster*. A trickster is a clever character who uses wits instead of strength.

words.d: a story told out loud and passed down over many years
a clever story character who wins by using wits instead of strength
a people of Ghana and nearby lands in West Africa

look.title: How Anansi Got the Stories
look.text: Anansi asks the Sky God for all the world's stories. The price is to capture a python, a leopard, a swarm of hornets and a fairy. Anansi uses a trick for each one. The Sky God keeps his promise. From then on, the stories belong to Anansi.
look.cite: Traditional Akan tale, retold in Gail E. Haley, A Story, a Story, 1970
look.prompt: What does this story show about how Anansi wins?

check.q: Which people first told Anansi stories?
check.why: The reading says Anansi stories come from the Akan people of Ghana.

check.q: What makes Anansi a trickster?
choices: He wins with clever tricks instead of strength
check.why: A trickster uses wits instead of strength, just as Anansi does.

check.q: How did Anansi stories reach Jamaica?
choices: Enslaved Africans carried them across the ocean
check.why: The reading says enslaved Africans carried the stories to the Caribbean and the Americas.

lessons.title: The Brothers Grimm
lessons.mainIdea: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected German folktales and published them in 1812.
reading: In the early 1800s, two brothers in Germany went looking for stories. Their names were Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm. They listened to neighbors, friends and storytellers. They wrote the tales down carefully.
In 1812, they published their first book of *fairy tales*. It included Hansel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood and Rapunzel. Many of the stories were darker than the cartoon versions you may know.

The brothers worried that these stories would be forgotten. Writing them down helped *preserve* them. Today their tales have been translated into well over a hundred languages. Movies and picture books still retell them.

words.d: a folktale with magic, like talking animals, witches or wishes
to keep something safe so it is not lost

look.title: Two Kinds of Storytelling
look.text: An Akan grandfather tells an Anansi story out loud. He changes his voice for each animal. The children join in. In Germany, Wilhelm Grimm sits at a desk. He writes a story in ink so it will be printed in a book.
look.prompt: What is one good thing about telling a story out loud, and one good thing about writing it down?

check.q: What did the Brothers Grimm do?
check.why: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected German folktales and published them.

check.q: Why did the brothers write the stories down?
choices: So the stories would not be forgotten
check.why: The brothers worried the stories would be forgotten, so writing them down helped preserve them.

check.q: Which story is a Grimm fairy tale?
check.why: Hansel and Gretel was in the Grimms' 1812 book, along with Little Red Riding Hood and Rapunzel.

lessons.title: The Monkey King
lessons.mainIdea: The Monkey King is the bold, magical hero of Journey to the West, a famous Chinese novel.
reading: A monkey bursts out of a stone egg on a mountaintop. He is fast, strong and very proud. He learns magic. He can leap across the sky on a cloud. His name is Sun Wukong, the *Monkey King*.

The Monkey King is a hero of *Journey to the West*. It is a Chinese novel written in the 1500s. Many scholars credit it to Wu Cheng'en. In the story, the Monkey King causes so much trouble in heaven that he is trapped under a mountain.

Later he is set free to protect a monk on a long trip to India. The monk is bringing back holy Buddhist writings. The Monkey King learns to use his power to help others. Operas, cartoons and video games still tell his adventures.

words.d: Sun Wukong, the magical monkey hero of Journey to the West
a famous Chinese novel from the 1500s about a monk's trip to India
a long made-up story written as a book

look.title: Anansi Meets the Monkey King
look.text: Anansi is small and wins by tricks. The Monkey King is strong and does magic. Both are clever. Both get into trouble. Anansi tricks others to get what he wants. The Monkey King learns to use his gifts to help a friend.
look.prompt: Which character would you want on your team, and why?

check.q: What is the Monkey King's name?
check.why: The Monkey King is Sun Wukong, the hero of Journey to the West.

check.q: In Journey to the West, whom does the Monkey King protect?
check.why: He is set free to protect a monk on a long trip to India to bring back Buddhist writings.

check.q: What does the Monkey King learn in the story?
choices: To use his power to help others
check.why: The reading says the Monkey King learns to use his power to help others.

lessons.title: How Culture Travels and Blends
lessons.mainIdea: Music, games and stories spread when people move, trade and share, and they often blend into something new.
reading: Think about everything in this chapter. Chess moved from India to Persia to Europe. Soccer sailed from England to Brazil. Anansi crossed the ocean to Jamaica. Culture travels when people move, trade and share.

When cultures meet, they often *blend*. Blend means to mix into something new. Flamenco blended Roma music with other sounds of Spain. K-pop blended Korean songs with American hip-hop. The new thing belongs to both.
Blending does not erase where something came from. Chaturanga became chess, but it is still India's gift. Knowing a thing's roots is a way to show *respect*. It honors the people who made it first.

words.d: to mix two or more things into something new
treating people and their ideas as important and worth care
the way of life of a group, including its food, music, games, stories and beliefs

look.title: Trace the Path
look.text: A Chicago family eats pizza from Italy, then plays a game of chess from India. They listen to K-pop from Korea and read a Grimm fairy tale from Germany. Before bed, their little brother asks for an Anansi story.
look.prompt: Pick two things from the family's evening. Trace where each one started and how it might have reached Chicago.

check.q: What does blend mean?
choices: To mix things into something new
check.why: To blend is to mix two or more things into something new, like K-pop mixing Korean songs and hip-hop.

check.q: Which is an example of culture traveling?
choices: Chess moving from India to Persia to Europe
A tree growing in one place
check.why: Chess moved from India to Persia to Europe as people traded and shared.

check.q: Why is knowing a thing's roots a way of showing respect?
choices: It makes the thing cost more
It keeps others from using it
It honors the people who made it first
check.why: The reading says knowing a thing's roots honors the people who made it first.
